items.title: Accessibility
items.summary: Accessibility is a contract this design system makes with every user — keyboard-only, screen-reader, low-vision, motor-impaired, or cognitively-loaded. The lib is built so that an app can ship accessibly by default; degrading that requires effort, not the other way around.

items.title: Accessibility scorecard
items.summary: Per-component accessibility status. Updated as components ship. Pass means the property is verified by tests, prop contracts, or PatternFly's own a11y guarantees. Partial calls out a known gap with a path to close.

items.title: Design for accessibility
items.summary: Most accessibility wins or fails happen at design time. Following these rules when defining brands, choosing colors, and laying out screens makes a11y the default, not a remediation step.

items.title: Develop for accessibility
items.summary: Code patterns and prop contracts that make a11y the default in apps built on this system. Most rules are enforced by TypeScript or PatternFly internals — the rest are quick disciplines.

items.title: PatternFly's accessibility
items.summary: This system is built on PatternFly 6 , which has its own multi-year a11y program. Most components used in this lib are either thin wrappers around PF components or compositions of them — so what PF guarantees, we inherit. This page is an honest map of what comes from where.

items.title: Testing your accessibility
items.summary: Automated tests catch the regressions; manual testing catches the subtle stuff. A real a11y workflow uses both. The repo ships some of this for you; the rest is on the consuming app.

items.title: Chat
items.summary: The AI prompt bar — where users type to talk to an assistant — and the surfaces it grows into. Example 1 is the bare pill (the same bar the Compass Example demo docks in its CompassMessageBar footer slot), with a soft pulsating glow on send. Example 2 wraps it in a colourful AI-indicator border that sweeps around the b

props.name: overlayContainer
props.description: A position:relative element the overlays (recent popover + full chat) portal into and anchor to. When omitted they render inline next to the bar.

props.name: placement
props.description: Default corner the full-chat panel anchors to on desktop (always inset from the corner). Users can move it at runtime via the panel's ⋮ menu.

props.name: labels
props.description: Override any user-facing copy — placeholder, headers, link text, and every aria label. Merged over the English defaults.

props.name: persist
props.description: Remember the chosen corner + panel size across reloads (localStorage). When off, the panel always opens at the defaults.

props.name: persistKey
props.description: localStorage key prefix used when persist is on.

props.name: onSend
props.description: Produce the assistant's reply to a sent message — wire your AI backend here. The thinking indicator shows until the returned value resolves. When omitted, a canned demo reply answers after a short delay.

props.name: initialMessages
props.description: Seed the conversation, e.g. history restored from your backend. ChatMsg is { role: "user" | "ai", text: string, at: Date }.

items.usage: AiAssistant is the lib's exported AI chat experience: a brandable prompt bar that renders inline wherever you place it, plus the surfaces it grows into — a transient recent-chat popover and a repositionable, resizable, searchable full-conversation panel (a modal below the sm breakpoint). Overlays portal into the `overlayContainer` element (position: relative) and anchor to its corners. Wire your backend via `onSend`; seed restored history via `initialMessages`; localise every string via `labels`. Styles ship in the lib stylesheet (`@golden-passport/ds-patternfly/styles`) — no extra CSS import.

examples.name: AssistantInShell
examples.description: The assistant docked in the app Shell: branded masthead + sidebar nav, content stage as the overlay container, and a live async onSend handler.

items.title: MCP
items.summary: The lib ships an MCP server — @golden-passport/ds-patternfly-mcp — that exposes the docs catalog (every Storybook story, plus foundations, recipes, and guidelines) to AI coding agents. Point your agent at the server and it can search the catalog, pull summaries, and link directly to Storybook instead of hallucinating c

items.title: Charts
items.summary: PatternFly Charts is a thin wrapper around Victory (Formidable's composable React chart library) — same API, PF6 theming, sensible defaults, and accessibility hooks baked in. From @patternfly/react-charts . Use it for dashboards, monitoring screens, and any product visualisation.

items.title: Area chart
items.summary: A filled line — emphasises cumulative volume over time. Use for a single series' total (run volume, request count); stack variants compare contribution across categories. For pure trend, prefer Line.

examples.name: AreaChart

items.title: Bar chart
items.summary: Discrete categorical comparison — counts per status, totals per region. Use vertical bars for short labels; switch to horizontal when labels are long or there are > 6 categories.

examples.name: BarChart

items.title: Box plot chart
items.summary: A statistical distribution chart — min, Q1, median, Q3, max per category. Use for latency distributions, error-rate spread, performance regression detection. PF6 doesn't ship a dedicated ChartBoxPlot wrapper, so compose Victory's VictoryBoxPlot directly inside a PF6 themed Chart .

examples.name: BoxPlotChart

items.title: Bullet chart
items.summary: A single-metric performance chart — actual value, target, qualitative bands (poor / acceptable / good). Compact: fits in a card or table cell. Use for SLA dashboards, budget vs actual, capacity usage with thresholds.

examples.name: BulletChart

items.title: Colors for charts
items.summary: PF6 ships ten named theme colours. Pass themeColor on any Chart wrapper to switch palettes — categorical (multi), monochrome (blue / green / etc), or semantic (status colours wired through Themes). Keep palettes consistent within a dashboard so users don't re-learn which series is which on each chart.

items.title: Donut chart
items.summary: A pie with a hole for centre text — “163 workflows” big number + slice breakdown. Cap at ~6 slices; beyond that it's legible as a Bar but unreadable as a donut. The hole is the killer feature: it puts the topline number front and centre.

examples.name: DonutChart

items.title: Donut utilization chart
items.summary: The single-metric variant of Donut — a percentage filled arc with a centred count. Use for “78% of disk used”, “62% of seats provisioned”. Pair with thresholds for at-a-glance warning / danger banding.

examples.name: DonutUtilizationChart

items.title: Legends
items.summary: The colour-to-series key. Drop a ChartLegend inside a chart, or pass legendData + legendPosition on the Chart wrapper and PF6 places it for you. Always include a legend when there's more than one series.

examples.name: Legends

items.title: Line chart
items.summary: The classic trend visualization — values over time. Use Line when emphasis is the rate of change; switch to Area when the cumulative total matters. Multiple series read cleanly in Line (cross-overs visible); Area stacks better for compositional totals.

examples.name: LineChart

items.title: Patterns
items.summary: SVG fill patterns (diagonal stripes, dots, crosshatch) as a second signal alongside colour. Use them when colour-blind accessibility matters, when printing in monochrome, or when the chart will be screen-shot to slides where reader colour fidelity isn't guaranteed.

examples.name: Patterns

items.title: Pie chart
items.summary: Composition of a whole — slices that sum to 100%. Prefer Donut over Pie when you have a meaningful centre value to surface; Pie is right when slice comparison itself is the point.

examples.name: PieChart

items.title: Resize observer
items.summary: Charts default to a fixed width + height in pixels. To make a chart fluid (fill its container, resize as the window changes), wrap it in a sized parent and let PF6's built-in containerComponent watch for resize via ResizeObserver . Pass height only; let width come from the container.

examples.name: ResizeObserver

items.title: Sankey chart
items.summary: Beta Flow visualization — values moving from one bucket to another. Use for funnel analysis (signups → active → paying), traffic routing (region → service → endpoint), and budget allocation. PF6 ships a beta Sankey via the ECharts wrapper ( @patternfly/react-charts/echarts ); a hand-rolled d3-sankey recipe is shown bel

examples.name: SankeyChart

items.title: Scatter chart
items.summary: Points on an X/Y plane — for distributions, correlations, and outlier detection. Use when each point is a discrete record and you want users to spot clusters or anomalies. Size / colour can encode a third dimension.

examples.name: ScatterChart

items.title: Skeletons
items.summary: The loading state for a chart — a placeholder that occupies the same footprint as the real chart so the page doesn't jump when data arrives. PF6 doesn't ship a chart-specific skeleton; compose with Skeleton shapes that mimic the eventual chart silhouette.

examples.name: Skeletons

items.title: Sparkline chart
items.summary: A miniature, axis-less Line / Area — sits inside a table cell or KPI tile to show recent trend at a glance. The point is shape, not values. PF6 doesn't ship a dedicated ChartSparkline ; compose with Chart + ChartArea and zero out the padding.

examples.name: SparklineChart

items.title: Stack chart
items.summary: Cumulative composition over a categorical or time axis — useful when you care about the total and the contribution of each segment. Works with both ChartBar and ChartArea children. Avoid when comparing segments to each other matters more than totals — use grouped Bar instead.

examples.name: StackChart

items.title: Themes
items.summary: PF6 charts ship a default theme that maps to PF6 design tokens. Set themeColor to switch palettes (blue, green, multi, etc); use getCustomTheme to override specific style props (stroke width, label fonts, padding). Define custom themes once at module scope — passing a fresh object each render trashes Victory's diffing.

examples.name: Themes

items.title: Threshold chart
items.summary: A line chart with horizontal threshold overlays — warning, danger, SLA targets. Renders the metric and the alert thresholds in the same view so users see breaches in context. Use for latency-vs-SLA, error-rate-vs-budget, any “we set a target; did we hit it?” chart.

examples.name: ThresholdChart

items.title: Tooltips
items.summary: Hover affordances that surface exact values. The two most-used patterns are ChartVoronoiContainer (hover anywhere in the plot area; nearest point wins) and createContainer("voronoi", "cursor") (voronoi + crosshair line for time-series). Bare per-point hover targets are pixel-thin and frustrating — avoid them.

examples.name: Tooltips

items.title: Component groups
items.summary: Component groups are pre-built compositions of PatternFly primitives that solve a specific UI problem out of the box — error pages, bulk-select dropdowns, page headers, skeleton tables. They sit one level above the core component library: less flexible than primitives, but faster to ship when you need a standard patter

items.title: Multi-content card
items.summary: A card that hosts multiple equally-weighted Card children in a row, optionally separated by dividers and toggled via an expandable footer. Use it for dashboard summary tiles where 2–4 sub-cards belong together (e.g. status / counts / health) without introducing a separate Grid.

items.title: Page header
items.summary: A standard top-of-page header — title, subtitle, optional breadcrumbs, an action menu, an icon, and a status label slot. Use it as the first child of every PageSection so titles render consistently across the app. For app-shell chrome (logo, nav), use Masthead instead.

items.title: Service card
items.summary: A standardized tile for a service / capability — icon, title, description, optional helper text and footer. Use it on landing pages and product hubs where users pick a service to enter. Always pair with Gallery for the responsive grid.

items.title: Bulk select
items.summary: A toolbar dropdown for selecting all items, none, or just the current page — wraps a Dropdown + a checkbox toggle and emits the user's choice as a typed value. Use it above any selectable list / table that paginates.

examples.name: BulkSelect

items.title: Close button
items.summary: A standardized X button — same icon, same hit-target, same aria-label across every dismissable surface. Use it on drawers, panels, toasts, and any custom dismissable widget where Modal's built-in close isn't available.

examples.name: CloseButton

items.title: External link button
items.summary: A Button preset for outbound links — sets component="a" , target="_blank" , rel="noopener noreferrer" , and renders a trailing external-link glyph. Use it whenever the link leaves your app — docs, runbooks, vendor portals.

examples.name: ExternalLinkButton

items.title: Responsive actions
items.summary: A toolbar action set that collapses into a kebab dropdown below a configurable breakpoint. Wraps PF6's OverflowMenu with a per-action persistence flag so primary actions stay visible and secondary ones move into the kebab on narrow viewports.

items.title: Error boundary
items.summary: React error boundary with a built-in error page UI. Wrap routes, top-level layouts, or risky widgets — when a child throws, the boundary catches it and renders a friendly error page instead of unmounting the whole app.

examples.name: ErrorBoundary

items.title: Error state
items.summary: A pre-built EmptyState variant for “something failed” screens — load failures, save failures, partial-render failures. Use it in place of an EmptyState when the screen represents an error rather than absence of data.

examples.name: ErrorState

items.title: Maintenance
items.summary: A scheduled-downtime page — title, body, start / end times, time zone, and an optional information link. Use it when a service is intentionally unavailable so the user understands it's planned, not broken.

examples.name: Maintenance

items.title: Missing page
items.summary: A standard 404 page — title, body, and a link back home. Wire this up as the catch-all route in your router.

examples.name: MissingPage

items.title: Unauthorized access
items.summary: A 403 / no-permission page — title, body, return-to-previous and go-to-landing actions. Use it whenever a logged-in user lands on a screen they don't have access to.

items.title: Unavailable content
items.summary: A “something on our side is down” page — a 5xx-style message with a status-page link. Use it for backend outages and dependency failures where retry inside the app won't help.

items.title: Warning modal
items.summary: A pre-built confirmation modal for destructive or dangerous actions — delete, disable, force-restart. Wraps Modal with sensible defaults (warning icon, danger CTA) and offers a checkbox-gate or type-to-confirm guard for high-risk operations.

items.title: Column management modal
items.summary: A pre-built modal for showing / hiding table columns — checkbox list, optional drag-and-drop reorder, untoggleable “always-on” columns. Wire it up to a kebab item in your table's toolbar.

examples.name: ColumnManagementModal

items.title: Field Builder
items.summary: A two-column repeater for dynamic form rows — env vars, tags, key/value pairs, conditions. Manages the add / remove / focus-management chrome; you supply the inputs via a render prop.

examples.name: FieldBuilder

items.title: List manager
items.summary: A reusable selectable + reorderable list — the visible body of a column-management or preferences modal. Use the standalone ListManager when you want to embed the same UI inline (e.g. inside a Drawer) rather than launching the full ColumnManagementModal .

examples.name: ListManager

items.title: Log snippet
items.summary: A small, alert-coloured block for inline error logs and stack traces. Use it inside detail panels, error states, or notification drawers when you want to surface a snippet of machine output without launching a full log viewer.

examples.name: LogSnippet

items.title: Shortcut grid
items.summary: A grid of keyboard-shortcut hints — “Cmd+K to search”, “G then I for inbox”. Use it inside a help panel or a “Press ? for shortcuts” modal so power users can discover and learn the keymap.

items.title: Beta
items.summary: A small “Beta” / “Preview” / “Tech preview” tag for features that aren't generally available. Not a separate PF component — the convention is a Label with a consistent colour and copy. The recipe below is what we use across the design system.

examples.name: Beta

items.title: Severity
items.summary: A standardized severity indicator — critical / important / moderate / minor / none / undefined. Use it in security dashboards, vulnerability scanners, alert triage UIs where severity needs to read consistently across screens.

items.title: Skeleton table
items.breadcrumb: Component groups/Status and state indicators/Skeleton table
items.summary: A pre-built skeleton placeholder for tables — same structure as your real Table , with shimmering bars instead of data. Use it during initial load so the layout doesn't shift when rows arrive.

items.title: Stale data warning
items.breadcrumb: Component groups/Status and state indicators/Stale data warning
items.summary: A tooltip-icon for objects that are nearing or past a freshness threshold — old check-in data, abandoned workflows, unupdated host inventory. Use it next to row titles in inventory tables so users see freshness at a glance.

items.title: Status
items.summary: A standardized icon + label pair for object state — Healthy / Degraded / Failed / Unknown. Pair with a popover or link variant when the state has explanatory detail (failure reasons, runbooks).

items.title: Tag count
items.breadcrumb: Component groups/Status and state indicators/Tag count
items.summary: A small clickable tag indicator with a count — “3 tags”. Use it in tables and lists where each row has tags but rendering them all inline would clutter the row. Click opens a popover / drawer with the full list.

items.title: Accordion
items.summary: Vertically stacked, expandable sections. Use for FAQs, settings groups, and any list where each row can carry a body of detail the user opens on demand. Pick single-expand when sections are mutually exclusive (only one open at a time); pick multiple-expand when users want to compare sections side-by-side.

examples.name: Accordion

items.title: ActionList
items.summary: A spacing/layout primitive for groups of action buttons. ActionList handles the gap; you supply ActionListItem s containing real Button s. Use ActionListGroup to cluster related actions with extra space between groups. Most-used flags: isVertical (stack top-to-bottom — used inside Compass sidebars), isIconList (tighter

examples.name: ActionList

items.title: Alert
items.summary: Inline status messages that report the outcome of a user action or a system event. Five severities — info / success / warning / danger (plus the unstyled custom ). Use isInline for in-content alerts; use AlertGroup + isToast for transient notifications anchored to the viewport.

examples.name: Alert

items.title: Avatar
items.summary: A user's photo or initials, typically rendered in a masthead, comment thread, or member list. Always carries an alt describing the person.

examples.name: Avatar

items.title: Back to top
items.summary: A floating button that appears after the user scrolls past a threshold and returns them to the top on click. Use on long documentation pages, infinite-scroll lists, or any view where scrolling back manually is tedious.

examples.name: BackToTop

items.title: Backdrop
items.summary: A semi-transparent overlay that dims the page behind a focused surface. Modal , Wizard , and AboutModal include their own backdrop — you rarely render this directly. Use it to build custom blocking overlays (full-page loaders, custom dialogs).

examples.name: Backdrop

items.title: Badge
items.summary: A small numeric or short-text indicator typically attached to another element — a tab title, a nav item, a button — to show a count or unread state. For status pills, use Label instead.

examples.name: Badge

items.title: Banner
items.summary: A page- or app-level status strip that sits flush with the top of the viewport (or directly under the masthead). Use for system maintenance windows, environment markers (“You're on staging”), beta tags, and degraded-service notices — information that applies to the entire app, not just the current screen. F

examples.name: Banner

items.title: Brand
items.summary: A logo image with PatternFly's sizing conventions and built-in responsive width support. Typically rendered inside a Masthead; the Shell shipped by this lib accepts it via the brandLogo prop. For multi-resolution / art-directed logos — where you want a different image (e.g. the icon-only mark) at narrow widths — pass &

examples.name: Brand

items.title: Breadcrumb
items.summary: A trail of links showing the user's place in the hierarchy. Renders as <nav aria-label="breadcrumb"> ; the last item is the current page and is not a link. Use it on pages nested three or more levels deep — shallower trees don't need it.

examples.name: Breadcrumb

items.title: Button
items.summary: The action primitive. Triggers a discrete operation when clicked or activated by Space/Enter. Use a button for actions; use a link (anchor) for navigation. The two are not interchangeable, even when they look the same.

examples.name: Button

items.title: Card
items.summary: The workhorse content tile — header, body, footer, optional actions / selection / expansion. Use cards for at-a-glance summary tiles (dashboards, gallery views), grouped settings panels, and anywhere a piece of content needs its own surface.

examples.name: Card

items.title: ClipboardCopy
items.summary: Single-line input with a copy button — the canonical “here's a value, click to copy” control. Use for credentials, ids, version strings, share URLs, install commands, and any value the user needs to paste somewhere else verbatim. For multi-line code snippets, use CodeBlock with ClipboardCopyButton instead.

examples.name: ClipboardCopy

items.title: CodeBlock
items.summary: A fenced code surface for snippets, configuration, and CLI output. Pair the body with optional CodeBlockAction buttons (copy, run, share) and an expandable section when the full snippet would dominate the page. Use for any content consumers will copy verbatim — YAML manifests, command lines, workflow expressions, JSON

examples.name: CodeBlock

items.title: Compass
items.summary: A slot-based application layout — header, optional start / end sidebars, main body, and footer. Use Compass when the app needs persistent rails around the main content (notes panel, table-of-contents sidebar, activity feed) rather than the standard Masthead + single-sidebar shape that <Page> gives you. Added in P

examples.name: Compass

items.title: Content
items.summary: Wraps prose-style content with PatternFly's typographic defaults — paragraphs, lists, blockquotes, links. Use it around any block of long-form text so spacing, line height, and link styling stay consistent without per-element tweaks.

examples.name: Content

items.title: DataList
items.summary: A row-based list with structured cells, optional checkboxes, actions, and per-row expandable detail. Use it as the pre-Table workhorse — when each row is more than a few cells of tabular data but doesn't need a sortable / filterable column header chrome. For dense tabular data, use Table from @patternfly/react-table in

examples.name: DataList

items.title: DescriptionList
items.summary: Term / definition pairs — the canonical “key facts” renderer. Use on detail screens, settings panels, and anywhere a fixed set of attributes need stacked or columnar presentation. Renders as a <dl> for proper screen-reader semantics.

examples.name: DescriptionList

items.title: Divider
items.summary: A horizontal or vertical rule used to separate blocks of content. Renders as a semantic <hr> by default — screen readers announce it as a separator, sighted users see a line.

examples.name: Divider

items.title: Drawer
items.summary: A side panel that slides in to reveal contextual content — detail views, edit forms, activity logs. Pushes the main content rather than overlaying it (use Modal for true overlays). Detail-on-list patterns and primary-detail layouts use this.

examples.name: Drawer

items.title: DualListSelector
items.summary: Two side-by-side lists with controls for moving items between them — Available on the left, Chosen on the right (or whatever roles you assign). Use for permission pickers, role assignment, membership management — anywhere the user needs to curate a set from a larger pool.

examples.name: DualListSelector

items.title: EmptyState
items.summary: The placeholder a list / table / view shows when it has no content yet. Three jobs: orient the user (icon + title), explain the state (body), and offer a way out (action). Use it for empty collections, no-results-after-filter, error states, and loading states.

examples.name: EmptyState

items.title: ExpandableSection
items.summary: A single “Show more” block — a collapsible region with a labelled toggle. Use for progressive disclosure within flat content: optional advanced settings, expanded detail in a list row, supporting context that doesn't need to be visible by default. For multiple stacked sections, use Accordion .

examples.name: ExpandableSection

items.title: FileUpload
items.summary: A single-file upload control. Supports browse-to-select, drag-and-drop, and inline content editing for text-formatted files (YAML, JSON, scripts). Use it for one-at-a-time uploads; for bulk uploads use MultipleFileUpload.

examples.name: FileUpload

items.title: MultipleFileUpload
items.summary: A drop zone for many files at once with per-file progress tracking. Use it for batch uploads — assets, document collections, log bundles. For single-file flows use FileUpload.

examples.name: MultipleFileUpload

items.title: Footer
items.summary: PatternFly 6 doesn't ship a dedicated PageFooter component. The canonical pattern is a final <PageSection component="footer"> at the bottom of the page, rendered as a <footer> landmark for assistive tech.

examples.name: Footer

items.title: Forms
items.summary: The Forms section collects every input control in the lib — text primitives , choice + toggle controls , grouped / composed inputs , and the date & time pickers . They all sit on the same DS field height ( 36px ) and share radius, focus, and motion dials, so a Form composed from any mix of them reads as one cohesive su

examples.name: FormControl

items.title: Checkbox
items.summary: A two- or three-state boolean control. Use checkboxes for independent on/off choices, multi-select lists, and indeterminate parent-of-children selections (e.g. "select all").

examples.name: Checkbox

items.title: Date and time
items.summary: The Date and time section collects every control for picking a moment — single dates, paired date + time, ranges, time-only, and relative waits. They all share the same lib calendar primitives (CalendarPanel, CalendarPopout, BottomSheet, useMobileViewport, date-format helpers) — carried by each downloadable example fil

items.title: CalendarMonth
items.summary: A standalone month-view calendar — the picker grid that DatePicker uses internally. Render it directly when you need a date selection inline (a scheduling sidebar, a date-range view) without the popover/text-input surface DatePicker adds.

examples.name: CalendarMonth

items.title: DatePicker
items.summary: A text input paired with a popover calendar. Users can type a date directly or pick from the calendar — both inputs stay in sync. Use it inside forms where a date is one of several fields. The lib defaults the display format to DD/MM/YYYY (rest-of-world convention); US-style and other formats are a one-prop swap.

examples.name: DatePicker

items.title: DateTimePicker
items.summary: PatternFly 6 doesn't ship a single "date and time" component — the recommended pattern is two paired controls: DatePicker for the day and TimePicker for the time, side-by-side under one FormGroup. This page shows the recipe.

examples.name: DateTimePicker

items.title: FuturePicker
items.summary: Two-tab control for scheduling future work. Wait collects a relative offset (days / hours / minutes) and emits an ISO-8601 duration like PT2H30M or P1DT4H . Specific date uses an inline PF6 CalendarMonth validated to disable today + any past day. Each tab keeps its own state so flipping back and forth doesn't lose work

examples.name: FuturePicker

items.title: TimePicker
items.summary: A text input for time-of-day selection with a popover suggesting common times in the configured step. Supports 12-hour and 24-hour modes; pick the one that matches your locale's convention.

examples.name: TimePicker

items.title: Form
items.summary: The container that organizes form fields with consistent spacing, label/helper-text positioning, and submit-button alignment. Compose with FormGroup , FormSection , FormHelperText , and ActionGroup rather than building any of those from scratch.

examples.name: Form

items.title: FormSelect
items.summary: A native HTML <select> with PatternFly styling. Use it for 5–20 known options where users don't need search. For longer or unfamiliar lists, use the typeahead-capable Select (Components/Menus/Select).

examples.name: FormSelect

items.title: HelperText
items.summary: Short, supplemental text — typically beneath a form field — to describe expected input, validation rules, or current validation status. Pair with form fields via aria-describedby so screen readers announce the guidance.

examples.name: HelperText

items.title: Inline edit
items.summary: A read-by-default field that switches to edit mode on demand — pencil to start, check to save, X to cancel. Use it for single-field metadata edits where opening a modal would be heavy: titles, owners, descriptions, tags. PatternFly ships this as a composed pattern in 6.4.3 (no dedicated component), so the recipe below

examples.name: InlineEdit

items.title: InputGroup
items.summary: A horizontal cluster of inputs and add-ons that read as a single control — username with @-prefix, search with scope picker, URL with copy button. Use it whenever a field needs an adjacent label, unit, action, or related control. For multi-row layouts, use Form instead.

examples.name: InputGroup

items.title: NumberInput
items.summary: A numeric text input with built-in stepper buttons. Best for small-range values where users may want to nudge by one — quantity pickers, replica counts, retry counts. For values driven by feel rather than precision, use Slider.

examples.name: NumberInput

items.title: Radio
items.summary: One selection from a small fixed list. Use radios when the user needs to see all options at once; for longer lists prefer FormSelect or Select.

examples.name: Radio

items.title: SearchInput
items.summary: A text input pre-styled for queries — built-in search icon, clear button, and submit handling. Reach for SearchInput whenever the user is filtering or searching a list, not just typing free-form text.

examples.name: SearchInput

items.title: Slider
items.summary: A bounded numeric input where the visual position itself communicates the value. Use it for "by feel" numbers — volume, opacity, contrast threshold — where exact precision matters less than relative position. For exact numeric entry, use NumberInput.

examples.name: Slider

items.title: Switch
items.summary: A boolean toggle that applies its change immediately — no submit button needed. Use a Switch when flipping the control should instantly take effect (notifications on/off, dark mode, feature flag). For boolean choices that wait for form submission, use a Checkbox.

examples.name: Switch

items.title: TextArea
items.summary: Multi-line text input. Use it for descriptions, comments, messages — anywhere users may write more than a single line. For a known-short single-line field, use TextInput.

examples.name: TextArea

items.title: TextInput
items.summary: Single-line text input. The most common form field — wrap in a FormGroup to get the label, helper text, and validation indicator wired up correctly.

examples.name: TextInput

items.title: TextInputGroup
items.summary: A composition primitive for text inputs that need additional UI inside the input frame — leading icons, trailing utility buttons, inline chips, status indicators, validation icons. Reach for it when a plain TextInput can't fit what you need into the same visual control. The group owns shared state (disabled, validated)

examples.name: TextInputGroup

items.title: ToggleGroup
items.summary: A pill-shaped row of mutually-exclusive (or independently toggleable) options — the canonical view-switcher / inline radio. Use for view-mode toggles (list / grid / table), filter modes, and small sets of related boolean settings.

examples.name: ToggleGroup

items.title: Hero
items.summary: A banner region for landing pages and feature spotlights — full-width container, optional background image / gradient per colour mode, content centred to a constrained body width. PF6 6.5+ (currently @beta ). Used at the top of marketing-style pages where the header chrome is <Masthead /> but the first scroll pan

examples.name: Hero

items.title: Hint
items.summary: A small contextual callout — typically introducing a new feature, explaining a workflow, or pointing users to documentation. Less urgent than an Alert; more substantial than HelperText.

examples.name: Hint

items.title: Hyperlink
items.summary: A real <a> styled with the brand's blue link tokens. Use it for navigation — changing URL, jumping between views, opening external sites. For actions that don't change URL (open dialog, save, delete), use Button with variant="link" .

examples.name: Hyperlink

items.title: Icon
items.summary: A wrapper that applies sizing and semantic color to an SVG icon. The icon glyphs themselves come from @patternfly/react-icons — Icon supplies the consistent sizing scale and brand-aware status tinting.

examples.name: Icon

items.title: Jump links
items.summary: A list of in-page anchors that scroll to specific sections — a table of contents for long pages. The active link tracks the currently-visible section as the user scrolls. Use on settings pages, long-form documentation, or any view broken into named sections.

examples.name: JumpLinks

items.title: Label
items.summary: A small inline tag for status, category, or metadata. Replaces the deprecated Chip component for tag-like uses. Default to status="info" for generic informational tags ("Beta", "Draft", "New"); reach for the color palette only when distinct user-assigned categories matter.

examples.name: Label

items.title: List
items.summary: A semantic <ul> / <ol> with PF6 styling. Use for prose-flow lists (in body content, FAQ answers, instructional steps) and as a building block for icon-led item lists. For interactive selection lists, use SimpleList ; for tabular data, use DataList / Table .

examples.name: List

items.title: LoginPage
items.summary: The full-page sign-in shell — brand panel on the left, form panel on the right (or stacked on small viewports), with built- in slots for social-login icons, sign-up link, forgot-password link, and footer policy links. Pair with LoginForm for the credential fields. Use as the entry shell of an app before the user has au

examples.name: LoginPage

items.title: Masthead
items.summary: The top bar of an app. Three slots: a left brand region (logo + optional sidebar toggle), a centre/right region for global actions, search, user menu and notifications. Renders as <header> for proper landmark semantics. The sidebar it toggles — push vs overlay, breakpoints, full-height drawers, glass — is documen

examples.name: Masthead

items.title: Application launcher
items.summary: A grid-style menu of applications — the typical “9-dot” launcher in a masthead. PF6 ships this as a Dropdown composition: a kebab/dot trigger + a DropdownGroup of icon items. Use to give users a quick switcher between sibling apps in a suite.

examples.name: ApplicationLauncher

items.title: Context selector
items.summary: A scoped switcher — change the active workspace / project / organisation without leaving the current view. Built on Select + a search input above the list, with the current selection reflected in the trigger label.

examples.name: ContextSelector

items.title: Custom menus
items.summary: Recipes built on the lib's Menu primitive that don't fit one of the higher-level wrappers ( Dropdown , Select ). Two common shapes: a search-filtered command palette, and a menu with a sticky footer for “view all” / save-state / clear- filter actions.

examples.name: CustomMenus

items.title: Dropdown
items.summary: A menu of actions opened by a trigger. Use for action menus (kebab in toolbars / cards), command lists (“Run”, “Duplicate”, “Delete”), and any click-to-open list of things to do . For value selection, use Select instead.

examples.name: Dropdown

items.title: Menu
items.summary: The base menu primitive — used directly for static menus, wrapped by Dropdown / Select / OverflowMenu for triggered menus. Use it directly when you want a menu that's always visible (settings panel, inline pickers) or when you need composition that the higher-level wrappers don't cover.

examples.name: Menu

items.title: Menu toggle
items.summary: The trigger element for menus — used by Dropdown , Select , and any custom menu pattern. Comes in variants (default / primary / secondary / plain), sizes, split-button shapes (action + checkbox), and stateful styling. Use it directly when you need a menu trigger that doesn't fit one of the higher-level wrappers.

examples.name: MenuToggle

items.title: Options menu
items.summary: A toggleable menu of toggleable settings — used for filter sets, display preferences, and any cluster of options the user keeps tweaking. Built on Select with hasCheckbox options for multi-select shapes; grouped sections for settings clusters.

examples.name: OptionsMenu

items.title: Select
items.summary: A menu for picking values — single or multi, with optional grouping, validation, and typeahead. The trigger label updates to reflect the selection. Use for form fields, switchers, and any choice list. For action menus, use Dropdown instead.

examples.name: Select

items.title: Modal
items.summary: A blocking overlay that demands attention. Use for confirmations, destructive actions, focused tasks, and errors that require a response. For non-blocking contextual content, use Drawer or Popover instead.

examples.name: Modal

items.title: Navigation
items.summary: Vertical or horizontal nav lists with active states, grouping, and nested sections. Renders as <nav> for landmark semantics. Pair with aria-label when the page has more than one nav region.

examples.name: Navigation

items.title: NotificationBadge
items.summary: A bell-icon trigger that surfaces unread / attention status — commonly placed in the masthead to open a NotificationDrawer. Three semantic variants ( read / unread / attention ) plus an optional unread count.

examples.name: NotificationBadge

items.title: NotificationDrawer
items.summary: The slide-in panel that hosts notifications — paired with NotificationBadge in the masthead, and surfaced via the Page.notificationDrawer slot. Use for system events, async job results, mentions, and any asynchronous status the user should be able to review at any time.

examples.name: NotificationDrawer

items.title: OverflowMenu
items.summary: A toolbar wrapper that collapses items into a kebab menu below a chosen breakpoint. Use it inside Toolbar / CardHeader when the row carries more actions than fit on narrow viewports — desktop sees the buttons, mobile sees the kebab + an overlay menu.

examples.name: OverflowMenu

items.title: Page
items.summary: The top-level layout shell. Composes Masthead , PageSidebar , and PageSection into the standard app skeleton — header bar, optional collapsible sidebar, scrolling main content. Use it as the outermost container of every app screen; the lib's own Shell is built on top.

examples.name: Page

items.title: Pagination
items.summary: Page-through controls for long collections — tables, lists, search results. Combines per-page sizing, prev/next, jump-to-page, and a “showing X–Y of Z” summary. Use the same component above and below a table for symmetric controls.

examples.name: Pagination

items.title: Panel
items.summary: A lightweight surface container — header, scrollable body, footer. Use it for self-contained content blocks inside a page (filter summaries, side notes, log streams). For data rows use DataList ; for top-level page sections use PageSection ; for elevated content with chrome use Card .

items.title: Popover
items.summary: A click-triggered floating panel anchored to a control. Use for contextual help, definitions, mini-forms, and any rich content that doesn't justify a modal. Unlike Tooltip , popovers are interactive — they can hold links, buttons, and form inputs.

examples.name: Popover

items.title: Progress
items.summary: A determinate progress bar with optional title, percentage, and status variant. Use for long-running tasks where you can express progress as a fraction of total — uploads, deployments, multi-step jobs. For indeterminate spinners (work-of-unknown-duration), use Spinner .

examples.name: Progress

items.title: ProgressStepper
items.summary: A multi-step progress indicator — each step has a status ( pending / info / success / warning / danger ) and one is marked isCurrent . Use for wizards, BPM workflow execution, deployment pipelines, onboarding flows — anywhere the user benefits from seeing where they are in a sequence.

examples.name: ProgressStepper

items.title: Sidebar
items.summary: A two-column layout primitive — a fixed-width SidebarPanel next to a flexible SidebarContent. Use it for in-page side panels: filter trails, settings menus, table of contents, secondary navigation. For app-level sidebars (the kind that holds primary Nav), use PageSidebar on Page instead — that's a different component m

examples.name: Sidebar

items.title: SimpleList
items.summary: A single-select list of items — the lightweight cousin of DataList . Use for in-page navigation lists, picker menus inside Drawers / Popovers, and side-rail selectors. Built-in keyboard navigation (arrow keys + Enter) and aria-selected wiring.

examples.name: SimpleList

items.title: Skeleton
items.summary: A placeholder shape that mimics the layout of content while it loads. Better than a spinner for first-page loads — gives users a sense of structure before data arrives, reduces perceived wait time.

examples.name: Skeleton

items.title: SkipToContent
items.summary: A keyboard-only escape hatch: an anchor that's visually hidden until it receives focus, then jumps screen-reader and keyboard users straight to the main content region. PF6 renders it as the first child of the page so a single Tab press surfaces it before any chrome. Required for WCAG 2.1 2.4.1 Bypass Blocks compliance

examples.name: SkipToContent

items.title: Spinner
items.summary: A loading indicator for short, indeterminate operations. Use it when something is happening but you can't communicate progress (no percentage, no step count). For known progress, use Progress instead.

examples.name: Spinner

items.title: Table
items.summary: The PF6 workhorse for tabular data — sortable, selectable, expandable, sticky-headerable. Lives in @patternfly/react-table (separate package from @patternfly/react-core ). Use Table for tabular data with column headers and any kind of column-level interaction; reach for DataList when each row is more like a card than a

examples.name: Table

items.title: Tabs
items.summary: Switch between sibling views without leaving the page. Use for related content that shares a heading — settings panels, detail views, dashboard subsections. For navigation between pages, use Nav instead.

examples.name: Tabs

items.title: Timestamp
items.summary: A locale-aware date / time renderer with built-in tooltip support. Use for any timestamp surfaced in the UI — “last run”, “created at”, “updated” — so dates get consistent formatting and a hover tooltip that surfaces the full date / timezone for context.

examples.name: Timestamp

items.title: Title
items.summary: A heading with PatternFly type-scale styling. The visual size is decoupled from the heading level — pick the level for the document outline (H1 → H6), pick the size for the visual hierarchy.

examples.name: Title

items.title: Toolbar
items.summary: The action / filter row that sits above tables and lists. Composes search, filter chips, sort, view toggles, and primary actions in a single horizontal bar that wraps gracefully on narrow viewports.

examples.name: Toolbar

items.title: Tooltip
items.summary: A small floating label that appears on hover or focus. Use it for short, supplemental hints — not for primary content. If a user must read it to understand the UI, it doesn't belong in a tooltip.

examples.name: Tooltip

items.title: TreeView
items.summary: A collapsible tree of nodes — file-browser style hierarchical navigation. Items can be selected, multi-selected, paired with icons, badges, or per-node action menus, and filtered by an external search input. Use for nested data: workspaces / projects / environments, file trees, taxonomies.

examples.name: TreeView

items.title: Truncate
items.summary: A long-string truncator with auto-tooltip. Use for filenames, ids, URLs, and any unbounded text rendered in width-constrained layouts (table cells, sidebars, breadcrumb segments). The full string is available on hover via PF's Tooltip.

examples.name: Truncate

items.title: Wizard
items.summary: A multi-step task runner with a step rail, per-step body, and a standard footer (Back / Next / Cancel / Submit). Use it for create-flows that have natural sub-steps where users need orientation (“step 2 of 5”) and the option to jump back. For single-question flows, use a regular Form inside a Modal instead.

examples.name: Wizard

items.title: Extensions
items.summary: Extensions are PatternFly packages that live outside @patternfly/react-core and ship larger, more opinionated building blocks — catalog tiles, data views, log viewers, quick starts, consoles, feedback modals. They're published as separate npm packages so you only pay for what you import.

items.title: Catalog item header
items.summary: The page header for a single catalog item — large icon, title, vendor line. Render it at the top of the catalog item's detail page so users know what they clicked into.

items.title: Catalog tile
items.summary: A single tile in a catalog grid — title, vendor, description, optional icon, badges, footer. Renders as a link when href is set; renders as a selectable card when paired with isSelected + onClick .

items.title: Catalog view
items.summary: A grid of selectable / linkable cards for catalogs — services, plugins, marketplace items. The pattern combines CatalogTile (the card), CatalogItemHeader (in-detail header), FilterSidePanel (left-rail facets), PropertiesSidePanel (right-rail metadata), and VerticalTabs (left-rail nav). All from @patternfly/react-catalo

items.title: Filter side panel
items.summary: The left rail of facet checkboxes for a catalog page — vendor, type, status, region. Pair FilterSidePanel with one or more FilterSidePanelCategory blocks; each category has a Show-X-more affordance baked in.

items.title: Properties side panel
items.summary: The right rail of metadata on a catalog detail page — version, maintainer, support level, expires-on. Pair PropertiesSidePanel with one or more PropertyItem children, and stack actions (Install, Subscribe) at the bottom.

items.title: Vertical tabs
items.summary: A left-rail tab list — common as the secondary nav inside a catalog item detail page (Overview / Configuration / Permissions / Logs). Less heavyweight than PageSidebar , cleaner than horizontal Tabs when you have ≥ 4 entries.

items.title: Overview
items.summary: A pre-wired Table + Toolbar + Pagination + Selection package — handles the boilerplate every product table reinvents. Use it when you want a drop-in modern data table with filters, selection, sort, pagination, and consistent UX across products. From @patternfly/react-data-view .

items.title: Table
items.summary: The table renderer for Data view — accepts columns + rows arrays, handles selection wiring, and dispatches head / body content for loading / empty / error states.

items.title: Toolbar
items.summary: The toolbar that sits above a Data view table — named slots for filters, bulk select, actions, view-toggle group, and pagination. Everything is a render-slot, so you stay in control of the inner components.

items.title: Log viewer
items.summary: A virtualised log-streaming component with ANSI colour support, search, line numbers, and dark/light themes. From @patternfly/react-log-viewer . Use it whenever you need to render > a few hundred lines of machine output without freezing the page. LogViewer mounts an off-screen <canvas> -style measurement layer

items.title: Quick starts
items.summary: Guided product tours rendered from declarative YAML / JSON. The package ships a catalog page (a grid of available tours), a drawer that walks the user through each step with markdown + screenshots, and a controller that persists progress to localStorage. From @patternfly/quickstarts . Quick starts wraps the entire app

items.title: React console
items.summary: A toolkit of remote-console viewers — Serial (xterm.js wrapper), VNC (noVNC), and Desktop (RDP-style placeholder). Used in OpenShift-style admin UIs where the user needs an in-browser terminal or graphical session into a VM. From @patternfly/react-console . These components depend on heavy runtime libraries and a live

items.title: User feedback
items.summary: A pre-built feedback / bug-report / mailing-list modal — same shape as Red Hat's product feedback flow. Configure each optional channel (feedback, bug report, mailing list, support case) by either passing a URL (redirect) or a callback (handle inline). From @patternfly/react-user-feedback .

items.title: Foundations
items.summary: Design foundations are the building blocks of the design system — the things every component is made of. They are intentionally opinionated so that any UI assembled from them looks cohesive, performs well, and stays accessible. This system layers on top of PatternFly 6 and is brandable via swappable token sets (e.g. Go

items.title: Colors
items.summary: Semantic tokens describe a color's role in the UI. Components reference these, never raw palette values, so re-skinning is a matter of swapping the brand. Each token resolves to a different value per color mode (currently: ). Switch the Mode toolbar above to see how each role adapts. The right-most number on each row i

items.title: Focus
items.summary: The visible focus indicator is the most important a11y feature most teams under-invest in. The lib normalises PF6's mixed default (inputs inner, buttons / menus outer) into one consistent system-wide style, configurable via <ThemeProvider focusRing="outer" | "inner"> .

items.title: Icons
items.summary: Icons come from @patternfly/react-icons (declared as a peer dependency). They inherit color from currentColor , so you set their color by setting CSS color on a parent — typically with one of our semantic icon tokens.

items.title: Motion
items.summary: Motion tokens describe how the system animates. Durations and easings are part of the brand contract so motion can feel different per brand (e.g. Golden Passport uses a softer, slightly slower set than the default).

items.title: Open UI Automation
items.summary: OUIA (Open UI Automation) is a small, cross-framework spec for stable test selectors. PatternFly 6 implements it: every OUIA-compliant component emits three attributes on its root — data-ouia-component-type , data-ouia-component-id , data-ouia-safe . Test runners locate elements by data-ouia-component-id without coupli

items.title: Radius
items.summary: Six corner-radius tokens, aligned to PatternFly 6's semantic scale. Use them via the --gp-radius-* CSS variables or pass through brand tokens — values shift per brand without component changes.

items.title: Responsive and mobile
items.summary: This system is mobile-first: every layout starts as a single column and progressively reveals more structure as horizontal space allows. Apps built on the lib inherit PatternFly 6's breakpoint scale; the lib's own components branch at one point — the md threshold (768px) — where the primary navigation pattern shifts fr

items.title: Spacers
items.summary: The spacing scale is used for padding, margin, gaps, and inset. Five steps cover the great majority of layout decisions; if you need something between, prefer the next-larger token over a custom value to keep rhythm consistent.

items.title: Theming
items.summary: Theming is three dimensions: the active brand (a typed token object), the active color mode (light or dark), and an optional glass surface treatment. All three are controlled by props on <ThemeProvider> (and by the matching toolbar toggles above) — switching any of them re-renders all downstream components withou

items.title: Typography
items.summary: Typography is sourced from the active brand. Two stacks: one for body , one for headings (defaults to body if unspecified). The scale below is a reference — the lib doesn't prescribe heading components today, leaving you free to use PatternFly's <Title> with these sizes.

items.title: Usage and behavior
items.summary: Cross-cutting rules every component in the system honors. These behaviors are guaranteed by the underlying PatternFly 6 primitives — wrappers in this lib never weaken them.

items.title: Layouts
items.summary: Layouts are PatternFly 6's set of structural primitives — small React components that compose into the page-level skeletons every BPM/automation app needs. They wrap CSS flexbox and grid with a token-aware API so spacing, breakpoints, and brand stay consistent across the system.

items.title: Bullseye
items.summary: Centers a single child both vertically and horizontally within its parent. The most common use case is empty states, loading spinners, and error screens where there's exactly one block of content and it should sit dead center of whatever space is available.

examples.name: Bullseye

items.title: Flex
items.summary: The general-purpose flex container. Wraps CSS flexbox in a token-aware API where spacing, direction, alignment, and justification are all set per breakpoint. Use it whenever a layout is essentially a row or column of items and none of the more specialized layouts (Level, Split, Stack) fit.

examples.name: Flex

items.title: Gallery
items.summary: A responsive grid of equal-width tiles. You specify the minimum tile width — the column count is computed by the browser at every viewport size. Use it for card grids, dashboards, and any collection where the items are interchangeable in shape.

examples.name: Gallery

items.title: Grid
items.summary: A 12-column grid with per-breakpoint span controls. Use it when items have distinct widths (a wide chart next to a narrow stat, a form with two columns of fields), and you want to express the layout in column units rather than pixels or percentages.

examples.name: Grid

items.title: Level
items.summary: A single horizontal row that distributes its children with justify-content: space-between . Use it for headers, footers, and any row where one or two items sit at the edges with space (or other items) between them.

examples.name: Level

items.title: Split
items.summary: A horizontal row where one item fills remaining space and the others stay intrinsic. The classic use is a sidebar + content area, or a row with a flexible label that expands to push trailing icons to the end.

examples.name: Split

items.title: Stack
items.summary: The vertical equivalent of Split — children stack top-to-bottom, and exactly one item can be marked isFilled to expand and consume remaining vertical space. The classic use is a page chrome layout: header, scrolling body, footer.

examples.name: Stack

items.title: Patterns
items.summary: Patterns are recipes — proven compositions of PF6 primitives that solve a recurring UX problem (bulk select, card view, primary-detail, password strength). They're not packages and they're not components. Each page documents the shape, the accessibility considerations, and ships a working demo you can copy.

items.title: Actions
items.summary: How to lay out action buttons on a page, in a row, or in a toolbar — one primary, a few secondaries, the rest in a kebab. The pattern keeps button hierarchy predictable across surfaces so users don't have to re-learn which button does the destructive thing in each screen.

items.title: Bulk selection
items.summary: The standard toolbar + checkbox triplet for “select many, act on many”. One BulkSelect dropdown for select-all / select-page / clear; per-row checkboxes for granular pick; bulk-action buttons in the toolbar that only appear when selection is non-empty.

items.title: Demo
items.summary: A responsive Gallery of Cards — the standard alternative to a Table when each row is more visual than tabular (catalog entries, dashboard tiles, image collections). Pair with a Toolbar for search + filters, and a Pagination below for large datasets.

items.title: Compass
items.summary: Patterns/Compass story

items.title: Dashboard
items.summary: The standard ops dashboard — KPI strip across the top, a wider chart card, a sidebar of status cards. Built from Gallery + Grid + Card ; no special dashboard component required. For the full app-shell version with masthead + nav, see AppShell .

items.title: Demo
items.summary: The standard filter toolbar — search input, one or more facet selects, removable filter chips that summarize the current state. Wire onClear on each chip so users can lift filters one at a time without re-opening the dropdown.

items.title: Demo
items.summary: An input group that produces, reveals, and copies a strong password. The standard shape: a read-only TextInput + regenerate / show / copy buttons. Generate via crypto.getRandomValues so the result is cryptographically random — never Math.random() .

items.title: Demo
items.summary: A live strength meter that updates as the user types — colour + label drive at-a-glance feedback; a per-rule checklist tells the user exactly what's missing. Both signals matter: colour alone fails WCAG, checklists alone leave the user guessing whether they're close.

items.title: Primary-detail
items.summary: A two-pane layout — a list of items on the leading edge (the primary), a content view on the trailing edge (the detail). Collapses to a single column with a “back to list” affordance below the md breakpoint. The headline pattern for record-browsing UIs: inbox, settings, user lists. See the live demo under P

items.title: Demo
items.summary: Shared body for the two PF6 primary-detail demos. The two variants differ only in chrome (mainContainerId on DashboardWrapper, colorVariant on DrawerContent, hasPadding on DrawerContentBody) — everything else is identical, so the body is parameterized rather than duplicated.

items.title: Demo
items.summary: PF6 ships RTL support via dir="rtl" + logical CSS properties ( margin-inline-* , padding-inline-* , inset-inline-* ). The lib's ThemeProvider takes a dir prop that flips the entire tree. Use the toolbar Direction control in this Storybook to flip the whole preview.

items.title: Shell
items.summary: Top-right masthead actions: notifications, help, settings, and a user dropdown (avatar + name + caret) — modelled on the PF6 reference demo patternfly.org/components/masthead/react-demos/utilities-and-user-dropdown-menu. Hooks live in a component so each render owns its dropdown open state.

items.title: Status and severity
items.summary: When a screen shows both severity (how bad?) and status (where are we in the workflow?), they're different signals and should look different. Severity uses a fixed ordinal scale (critical → minor); Status uses a fixed health scale (healthy → failed); Label handles everything else (tags, versions, products).

items.title: Utility classes
items.summary: PatternFly 6 ships a set of single-purpose CSS classes for the most common one-off styling needs — alignment, spacing, display, background color, and so on. The lib bundles them into its main stylesheet so you can use them directly in any consumer app without extra installs.

items.title: Accessibility
items.summary: Three classes for managing what is visible to sighted users versus assistive technology. Use them sparingly — usually a properly structured component is better than hiding things — but they are essential for skip links, off-screen labels, and breakpoint-driven UI swaps.

items.title: Alignment
items.summary: Logical-property text alignment. start and end respect writing direction (LTR vs RTL), so they work correctly in both English and Arabic without overrides.

items.title: Background color
items.summary: A small set of semantic background tones for cases where you need a quick surface treatment without authoring a component. These adapt to the active color mode automatically.

items.title: Box shadow
items.summary: Three elevation levels (sm, md, lg) and an edge variant for each side. Use sparingly — shadows compete for visual hierarchy, and the system relies more on borders and surface tone than on elevation.

items.title: Display
items.summary: Set the CSS display property without writing styles. Combined with the responsive suffix, these are the workhorses of mobile-first layouts — show as block on mobile, swap to flex at the md breakpoint, that sort of thing.

items.title: Flex
items.summary: Single-purpose classes for flex containers and their items. For most layouts, prefer PatternFly's Flex component — but when you need one-off alignment or a quick toolbar row, these utilities are faster than writing inline styles.

items.title: Float
items.summary: Logical-property floats. Float layouts are rare in modern UI — flexbox or grid almost always do a cleaner job — but for embedding a small image or icon inline with prose, these are the right tool.

items.title: Sizing
items.summary: Width and height in fixed percentage steps and viewport units. The percentage scale (0/25/33/50/66/75/100) covers the great majority of layout fractions; reach for raw CSS only when you need something between.

items.title: Spacing
items.summary: Margin and padding on the spacer scale, for every side and direction. The largest set of utilities the system ships — use them for one-off adjustments, but if you find yourself stacking three or four on the same element, the right move is usually a custom class.

items.title: Text
items.summary: Font family, size, weight, color, and wrapping. For body copy and headings, prefer the system's typography tokens ( --gp-font-* ) — these utilities are for one-off labels and inline emphasis.
